7.text: When bountifully fed, the dogs are quite unwearying, and can make long

8.text: runs for twenty successive days with but two daily rests. Their feet, however,

9.text: are very sensitive. Uneven ground with clods of hard snow, for instance; a

10.text: moss pasture recently left by a reindeer-herd; or rough, bare ice in late spring, —

11.text: will make their feet bleed, and rapidly disable them. Sore feet heal slowly,

12.text: though a well-trained dog sometimes keeps pace with the team when all its

13.text: feet are bleeding. Occasionally small boots of curried reindeer-skin (Fig. 27).

14.text: are put on the sore feet, though many dogs cannot

15.text: endure them, and will tear them off as soon as started

16.text: on the journey. Frost-bites of the groins are still worse,

17.text: since, even after recovery, the dog remains weak, and

18.text: susceptible to cold. The drivers, when caught on the

19.text: road by a severe tempest or even by a cold, contrary

20.text: wind, protect the dogs with strips of soft skin tied around

21.text: the groins (Fig. 28). The suckling females have square

22.text: strips of skin tied over their bellies for the same purpose.

23.text: When resting for a night, the dogs are usually

24.text: unharnessed, but are tied up with a halter. Sticks or

25.text: pieces of horn about thirty centimetres long are fastened

26.text: to the dog-collars. The ends of these sticks are tied

27.text: by short lines to stakes or to the sledges. The sticks

28.text: are long enough to prevent the dog from gnawing the

29.text: thong fastenings at the other end. Iron chains bought from traders or made

39.text: otherwise, without freedom of motion, they would be in danger of being buried

40.text: in the snow and stifled, especially when they are too tired to stand up every

41.text: little while, and shake off the snow.
